I published this theme on Sunday and I wasn't really expecting it to get so much attention so quickly, so I haven't yet put together documentation. In the meantime, this post will act as a rough FAQ. I will keep updating it as I answer specific questions.

How do I get Cashmere on my subverse?

See here.

What is Sass?

Sass is a CSS preprocessor. It takes a syntax which is different from CSS and processes it into valid CSS that your browser understands.

What is SCSS?

While Sass is the name of the program, it's also the name of the original Sass syntax. I'm using the newer, and more common, Sass syntax called SCSS. SCSS is completely compatible with CSS. If it's valid CSS, you can put it in an SCSS file and it works fine, but you can also add Sass features to it. When I say Sass, I'm referring to the program, not the syntax.

How can I get started with using Cashmere's SCSS files?

I've attempted to answer this question here. Koala is open-source, cross-platform, and easy to use.

Also see my guide on using the color variables.

How do I add a sidebar or banner image?

These are planned features, but there is currently no simple way of doing this.

Can I also use Cashmere on other subverses?

Important: Cashmere was never intended to be used this way. In fact, I don't recommend that you do this because it can mess up a lot of pages on Voat. The only reason this answer is here is because I got a couple questions about it. It's not an advertised feature.

It's possible (with Firefox at least).

  • Install the extension Stylish and create a new style.

  • Put the Cashmere CSS inside this rule:

@-moz-document url-prefix("https://voat.co/v/") {

}
  • Disable custom styles in your account settings.
It's also possible to use Cashmere in Chrome. There's a Stylish extension and the rest of the process is the same :)

Nevada legalized medical marijuana in 2000. It is now 15 years later, and there are still no legal medical marijuana (MM) dispensaries open and serving the public. What is wrong?

First of all, this was a ballot proposal only. What this means is that the onus is then on their representatives to clarify this by actually drafting and passing the subsequent law, and until that time only the ballot proposal is kind of in a quasi-state of "law" where it's legal but with confused clarity. Ironically the best explanation of this is not this ridiculously slanted opinion piece, but from a website called potguide. This act also limited the number of plants grown even for businesses, inadvertently, and the police have continued to raid people for growing plants.

Basically, the actual law detailing the results of "Question 9" was never written in spite of my best attempts to find information on it. The reason there aren't dispensaries isn't due to over-regulation, the reason is the current total lack of precise and clear explanation that would give businesses protection under law for operating within those limits. NO business is suicidal enough to begin in such a precarious position, and the only law I could find subsequent to this is referenced on that potguide website:

The expectation is that when Nevada voters head to the ballot boxes in November of 2016, some clarity will arise. At that time, Nevada residents will determine whether their state should legalize marijuana without restrictions. Until then, there is a gray area regarding weed distribution.

Now a lawyer with more access to this information could probably clarify. As it stands, I obviously did more research into the subject than the article writer within the 20 minutes it took me to write this.

Shadow of Mordor has released for Linux!

I'm so happy for this. I was under the impression that this release was delayed for at least another month or two. Surprise games - such a great way to start the day. :)

(now to wait for my crappy 'net connection to pull down 41 gigs....)
So... who ported this, and how is the port? Nice and all that it's ported, but if it that emu wrap crap that sucks (example original release of Witcher 2) I want to know a head of time.

It's ported by Feral Interactive, who only does native ports. I haven't gotten it yet so I don't know about the quality of Shadow of Mordor specifically, but their previous Linux ports (XCOM: EU and Empire: Total War) are pretty good.

This port is like hot sex, full native OpenGL code. In fact, they had to use 4.3 to get everything working. Given OSX only goes up to 4.1 for people running Yosemite they even went through and coded completely different opencl shaders for it. On Linux they showed us the love and gave us the native 4.3 extensions to get the rendering features parity with the windows version instead of just giving us their OSX sloppy seconds. I went through and compared the visual options between Windows/Linux and they are 100% parity. The performance delta for me on my GTX 980 is about 3% give or take. In some cases I'm seeing higher framerates in the Linux version.

This is not only a good port, but perhaps the best damn version of the game. They put that much work into it. This is how Linux games should be done.

Hats off to Feral, bravo, a full round of applause. They just showed the whole dev scene how its done. This game, right now, might just well be the best example of badass graphics coding ever seen outside of Epic's own UE4 work. I hope this points out just how good this port is.
